explanations.answer: That they had died in Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The whole congregation says, "If only we had died in the land of Egypt…" (Numbers 14:2). They add a second wish, that they had died in this wilderness. I think that's what a grumble sounds like when it's been simmering all night.

explanations.answer: That they had stayed at Mount Sinai
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but Sinai never comes up in what they say. The congregation grumbles against Moses and Aaron, Israel's leaders, and says they wish they had died in Egypt or in this wilderness. Both wishes are about dying, so it's a pretty heavy grumble.

explanations.answer: That they had picked different spies
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd go there, since the spies just gave their report. But the people never say a word about picking different spies. They tell Moses and Aaron, Israel's leaders, they wish they had died in Egypt or in the wilderness.

Yes, that's what they say. They ask, "Why is the LORD bringing us into this land to fall by the sword?" (Numbers 14:3). I think fear is doing the talking here. When fear grabs the microphone, it doesn't hand it back quick.

The people really do say this. Numbers 14:3 has them asking, "Why is the LORD bringing us into this land to fall by the sword?" So the statement is true. They said it right to Moses and Aaron, loud enough for everybody.

You got it, baker. They say, "Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt." (Numbers 14:4). They say it to one another, so this plan is coming from the crowd. Nobody asked Moses for his opinion on it.

Close, since scouts are what got everybody worked up. But the people don't ask for a new scout. They say, "Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt." (Numbers 14:4). Nobody wants more exploring at this point.

A guard sounds sensible, but it isn't what the people say. In Numbers 14:4 they say, "Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt." The word is leader. Nobody in this crowd is asking for a security detail.

That's right. Joshua and Caleb say, "The land we passed through and explored is an exceedingly good land." (Numbers 14:7). Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh were two of the spies, so they're speaking from what they saw. Same trip, very different review.

Dangerous is how the others told it, but not these two. Joshua and Caleb, who explored the land with the other spies, say it is an exceedingly good land (Numbers 14:7). They saw the same hills and walked the same ground. They just came back with a different word.

Crowded makes sense if you've been listening to the scary reports. But Joshua and Caleb never say that. They say, "The land we passed through and explored is an exceedingly good land." (Numbers 14:7).

Yes, baker. Joshua and Caleb say, "If the LORD delights in us, He will bring us into this land, a land flowing with milk and honey, and He will give it to us." (Numbers 14:8). The one doing the bringing and the giving is the LORD. That's why they keep pointing at Him and not at the crowd.

Moses and Aaron are right there, facedown in front of everyone at that moment. But Joshua and Caleb don't name them as the ones who will bring Israel in. They say the LORD will bring them into the land and give it to them (Numbers 14:8).

Tribal leaders don't come up in what Joshua and Caleb say. They say, "…He will bring us into this land, a land flowing with milk and honey, and He will give it to us." (Numbers 14:8). The "He" there is the LORD.

Not quite. Joshua and Caleb never brag about Israel's army. They say, "Their protection has been removed, and the LORD is with us." (Numbers 14:9). The confidence is in the LORD being with them. It's not about how strong the army is.

That's right, baker. Joshua and Caleb never say a word about the army's strength. They say, "Their protection has been removed, and the LORD is with us." (Numbers 14:9). All their courage sits on that last part.

Yes, that's what happens. "The whole congregation threatened to stone Joshua and Caleb." (Numbers 14:10). Two men tell the truth about a good land, and the crowd picks up rocks in its mind. Tough crowd, baker.

That would be a nice twist, but it's not what happens. The whole congregation threatens to stone Joshua and Caleb (Numbers 14:10). The crowd had already talked about appointing a leader, though, and it wasn't going well for these two.

explanations.answer: They ask to see the fruit
explanations.explanation: The fruit did show up earlier, when the spies showed the people the fruit of the land (Numbers 13:26). But here nobody asks to see it. The whole congregation threatens to stone Joshua and Caleb (Numbers 14:10).

That's the word, baker. The LORD asks, "How long will they refuse to believe in Me, despite all the signs I have performed among them?" (Numbers 14:11). The signs were right there for them to see. The LORD is asking why that still isn't enough.

Rejoice would be a nice word, but it's not the one here. The LORD asks how long they will refuse to believe in Him, despite all the signs He has performed among them (Numbers 14:11). The word is believe.

Walking they'd done plenty of, so it's an easy one to grab. But the LORD's question is about how long they will refuse to believe in Him, despite all the signs He has performed among them (Numbers 14:11). The missing word is believe.

You've got it. Moses says, "The Egyptians will hear of it, for by Your strength You brought this people from among them." (Numbers 14:13). He answers with a plea for the people. He doesn't take the offer to become a greater nation.

The Philistines don't come up in Moses' prayer. He says, "The Egyptians will hear of it, for by Your strength You brought this people from among them." (Numbers 14:13). The Egyptians are the ones God brought the people out from.

The Moabites never get a mention in Moses' prayer. He says the Egyptians will hear of it, for by the LORD's strength He brought this people from among them (Numbers 14:13). So the Egyptians are the ones Moses names.

Yes, that's right. Moses says the nations would say, "Because the LORD was unable to bring this people into the land He swore to give them, He has slaughtered them in the wilderness." (Numbers 14:16). Moses is telling the LORD what the nations who have heard of His fame would say. It's a pleading kind of prayer.

Moses really does say it. He tells the LORD the nations would say, "Because the LORD was unable to bring this people into the land He swore to give them…" (Numbers 14:16). So the statement is true. Moses is describing what the nations who have heard of the LORD's fame would say.

That's the word, baker. Moses prays, "Pardon, I pray, the iniquity of this people, in keeping with the greatness of Your loving devotion…" (Numbers 14:19). He asks for pardon based on how great the LORD's loving devotion is. He doesn't point to anything the people did to earn it.

Remember sounds like a prayer word, but it's not the one here. Moses prays, "Pardon, I pray, the iniquity of this people, in keeping with the greatness of Your loving devotion…" (Numbers 14:19). The word is pardon.

Measure is a funny one, but Moses doesn't ask for that. He says, "Pardon, I pray, the iniquity of this people, in keeping with the greatness of Your loving devotion…" (Numbers 14:19). The loving devotion is the thing that's great, and the request is for pardon.

Yes. The LORD replies, "I have pardoned them as you requested." (Numbers 14:20). Moses asked, and the LORD answered. It's a good moment to let out a breath, because the next part of the story gets heavy.

The LORD really does say it. He replies to Moses, "I have pardoned them as you requested." (Numbers 14:20). So the statement is true. The story keeps going from there, and some hard words are still ahead.

explanations.answer: None of them will see the land
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, "not one will ever see the land that I swore to give their fathers." (Numbers 14:23). These are the men who saw His glory and the signs, and still tested Him ten times (Numbers 14:22). It's a heavy verse, and the LORD means it.

explanations.answer: They will lead the way in
explanations.explanation: I wish it went that way, but it doesn't. The LORD says none of those men will ever see the land He swore to give their fathers (Numbers 14:23). Nobody in that group leads the way in.

Egypt is what the people were asking for, but it's not what the LORD says. He says not one of those men will ever see the land He swore to give their fathers (Numbers 14:23). Then He tells them to turn back and head for the wilderness along the route to the Red Sea (Numbers 14:25).

That's him, baker. The LORD says, "But because My servant Caleb has a different spirit and has followed Me wholeheartedly…" (Numbers 14:24). Caleb son of Jephunneh was one of the spies who said the land was good. The LORD calls him His servant.

Aaron is in this scene with Moses, but he's not the one the LORD singles out here. The LORD says, "But because My servant Caleb has a different spirit and has followed Me wholeheartedly…" (Numbers 14:24). Caleb is the name.

Eleazar doesn't show up anywhere in this passage. The LORD names Caleb: "But because My servant Caleb has a different spirit and has followed Me wholeheartedly…" (Numbers 14:24). Caleb is the man He singles out.

That's right. The LORD says, "…turn back tomorrow and head for the wilderness along the route to the Red Sea." (Numbers 14:25). He also mentions the Amalekites and Canaanites living in the valleys. Those are the people living in the land.

The LORD really does say that. He tells them, "…turn back tomorrow and head for the wilderness along the route to the Red Sea." (Numbers 14:25). So the statement is true. It's a change of direction for the whole camp.

explanations.answer: Exactly what He heard them say
explanations.explanation: You've got it. The LORD says, "I will do to you exactly as I heard you say." (Numbers 14:28). They had said they wished they had died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:2). Moses and Aaron are told to pass this along, so the people hear it from them.

explanations.answer: Lead them into the land at once
explanations.explanation: That's not what He says. The LORD says, "I will do to you exactly as I heard you say." (Numbers 14:28). He then says their bodies will fall in this wilderness, so no quick walk into the land is coming.

explanations.answer: Let them rest at Kadesh awhile
explanations.explanation: Kadesh doesn't come up in this passage, and neither does a rest. The LORD says, "I will do to you exactly as I heard you say." (Numbers 14:28). What follows is that their bodies will fall in this wilderness (Numbers 14:29).

Not quite, baker. The LORD says it reaches further than the spies: "Your bodies will fall in this wilderness—all who were numbered in the census, everyone twenty years of age or older—because you have grumbled against Me." (Numbers 14:29). The men who gave the bad report get their own mention a little later, when a plague strikes them (Numbers 14:37).

That's right. The LORD says, "Your bodies will fall in this wilderness—all who were numbered in the census, everyone twenty years of age or older—because you have grumbled against Me." (Numbers 14:29). So it's far more than the spies. It's everybody counted who was twenty or older.

Yes. The LORD says, "But I will bring your children, whom you said would become plunder, into the land you have rejected—and they will enjoy it." (Numbers 14:31). The people had said their children would become plunder (Numbers 14:3). The LORD says those same children will enjoy the land.

Servants don't come up in this verse. The LORD says, "But I will bring your children, whom you said would become plunder, into the land you have rejected—and they will enjoy it." (Numbers 14:31). The children are the ones He names.

The other spies aren't the answer. The men who brought out the bad report were struck down by a plague (Numbers 14:37). The LORD says it's the people's children He will bring into the land (Numbers 14:31).
That's it, baker. The LORD says, "you shall bear your guilt forty years—a year for each day" (Numbers 14:34). Forty days of spying became forty years. That's a long time to be on the road.
A month sounds long, but it's not enough here. The LORD says, "…you shall bear your guilt forty years—a year for each day…" (Numbers 14:34). It's a year for each of the forty days.
A week of guilt for each day would be a lot shorter than what the LORD says. He says, "…you shall bear your guilt forty years—a year for each day…" (Numbers 14:34). So it's a year, not a week.

Yes, baker. "Of those men who had gone to spy out the land, only Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh remained alive." (Numbers 14:38). The rest were struck down by a plague before the LORD (Numbers 14:37). Joshua and Caleb are the two who said the land was good.

The text really does say it. "Of those men who had gone to spy out the land, only Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh remained alive." (Numbers 14:38). So the statement is true. The others were struck down by a plague (Numbers 14:37).

explanations.answer: Go to the place the LORD promised
explanations.explanation: That's what they say. "We have indeed sinned," they said, "but we will go to the place the LORD has promised." (Numbers 14:40). They got up early the next morning to do it. The LORD had told them to turn back toward the wilderness the day before (Numbers 14:25), though.

explanations.answer: Search the hills for fresh water
explanations.explanation: Water isn't mentioned in this passage. The people say, "We have indeed sinned, but we will go to the place the LORD has promised." (Numbers 14:40). That's where they're heading.

explanations.answer: Bury the men from the plague
explanations.explanation: That's a thoughtful guess, but the text doesn't say that. They head up toward the ridge of the hill country, saying, "We have indeed sinned, but we will go to the place the LORD has promised." (Numbers 14:40).

explanations.answer: The LORD is not among them
explanations.explanation: Yes. Moses says, "Do not go up, lest you be struck down by your enemies, because the LORD is not among you." (Numbers 14:42). The reason is the LORD's absence, not how big the enemy is. Moses says it plainly and doesn't dress it up.

explanations.answer: Their army is far too small
explanations.explanation: Moses never says anything about the size of the army. He says, "Do not go up, lest you be struck down by your enemies, because the LORD is not among you." (Numbers 14:42). The reason he gives is that the LORD is not among them.

explanations.answer: The cities are too well fortified
explanations.explanation: That's what the spies' report was about earlier (Numbers 13:28). But Moses gives a different reason here. He says, "Do not go up, lest you be struck down by your enemies, because the LORD is not among you." (Numbers 14:42).

Not this time. The text says they went up "though neither Moses nor the ark of the covenant of the LORD moved from the camp." (Numbers 14:44). The people went up without either one. It matches what Moses had told them (Numbers 14:42).

That's right, baker. The people went up to the ridge "though neither Moses nor the ark of the covenant of the LORD moved from the camp." (Numbers 14:44). Moses and the ark stayed put. The people went up on their own.

That's the place. The Amalekites and Canaanites "attacked them, and routed them all the way to Hormah." (Numbers 14:45). The Amalekites and Canaanites were the people living in that part of the hill country. It's just what Moses warned them about.
Jericho is a famous name, but it's not in this verse. The Amalekites and Canaanites attacked Israel and routed them all the way to Hormah (Numbers 14:45). Hormah is the place named.
Joppa isn't in this passage. The text says the Amalekites and Canaanites came down, attacked them, and routed them all the way to Hormah (Numbers 14:45). That's the place the story ends on.
